units.translation: 257-62a. We are going to Orchomenus: through these words Argus says that the things told to them by Phineus (II 421) were true; for there is another voyage leading outside, which the Egyptian priests indicated. For Argus knew those regions. Therefore he says: 'Indeed, having used the innermost route, by which we also were traveling to Orchomenus, proceed.' L
12 ἐν τοῖς Ἀργοναύταις in L : τοὺς -ας in P

b. For there is another voyage: Herodorus in his Argonautica (31 fr. 10 J.) says that they came down through the same sea by which they went to Colchis. Hecataeus of Miletus (1 fr. 18a J.) says that they passed from the Phasis into the ocean, then from there into the Nile, and from there into our sea. Artemidorus of Ephesus (fr. 136 Stiehle Phil. 11, 1856, 236) says this is false; for the Phasis does not join the ocean, but flows down from mountains. Eratosthenes in the third book of his Geography (fr. III B 74 Berger) says the same. Timagetus in the first book of On Harbours (fr. 1 M. IV 519) says that the Phasis flows down from the †Celtic† mountains, which are in Celtica, then empties into the Celtic lake, and after this the water divides into two, and one part flows into the Euxine Sea, the other into the †Celtic† sea; and through this mouth the Argonauts sailed and came to Tyrrhenia. Apollonius follows him. Hesiod (fr. 64 Rz.²) and Pindar in his Pythian odes

(IV 25 sq.) and Antimachus in his Lyde (fr. 12 B. II 291) say that they came through the ocean to Libya, and carrying the Argo into our sea they arrived.

c. Not yet of the Danaans: many say that the Egyptians are the most ancient, but Herodotus (II 2) says the Phrygians. Mysemes in the first book of his Aegyptiaca (M. IV 369) and Leon in the first book of his work Against his Mother (fr. 1 M. II 331) and Cnossus in the first book of his Geography of Asia (M. III 158) say that the Egyptians are the most ancient of all.
